01 · Title — Why I research this problem

Behind the Route

Making the invisible networks of urban food delivery perceptible

As a Columbia University student, I often order food delivery. The app shows one route and one estimated arrival time, but the real journey is shaped by traffic, weather, restaurant waiting, rider decisions, and campus access. This mismatch between a clean interface and a complicated delivery experience is the starting point of my project.

Urban food deliveryCritical visualizationPlatform labor
02

02 · Research questions — What do I want to know?

This mismatch leads to four connected research questions:

The questions move from understanding what is hidden, to examining how the route is produced, and finally to considering how it can be visualized responsibly.

01

Omission

What does the interface omit?

Waiting, detours, access restrictions, risk, uncertainty, and rider decisions often disappear from the customer interface.

02

Production

How is the route actually produced?

It is jointly shaped by platform systems, restaurant operations, rider judgment, streets, buildings, weather, and local rules.

03

Revelation

How can design reveal the hidden relationships behind it?

Route comparison, layered mapping, spatial analysis, and interaction connect the visible line to the systems that produce it.

04

Accountability

How can evidence be represented responsibly?

The project distinguishes public data, field observation, modeled information, uncertainty, and missing evidence.

OmissionProductionRevelationResponsible evidence

03 · Keywords — What is the project about?

Five terms turn a familiar experience into a focused research framework.

To make these questions more precise, I define the project through five key terms: Food delivery is the research object. The route is the spatial entry point. Invisible infrastructure is the hidden system. Platform labor represents the human experience. And critical visualization is the method.

04 · Intersecting fields — How can I study it?

Movement, power, and representation frame the delivery route.

To study this system, the project connects three larger concerns: movement, power, and representation: Computational design and urban logistics help analyze movement through the city. Platform urbanism and labor studies reveal who controls the route and who bears the hidden costs. Critical cartography and infrastructure studies question what maps show and what they leave invisible. Together, these perspectives redefine the delivery route as more than a line between two locations.

05 · Historical lineage — How did today’s delivery network emerge?

From local food supply to algorithmic instant delivery.

To understand why food delivery has become automated and invisible, I trace its historical development: from local food supply and industrial logistics to telephone ordering, digital platforms, and algorithmic dispatch. As delivery becomes faster and more efficient, its infrastructure and labor become increasingly hidden from customers. This reflects the idea of partial knowing: computation can organize and predict complex systems, but it cannot fully represent lived experience, social context, and invisible labor.

Local and visible coordinationDistributed and automated coordination

06 · Community of practice — Who is working here, and where do I stand?

Who investigates, regulates, experiences, and builds the delivery system?

This community of practice shows who shapes contemporary food delivery systems. Forensic Architecture and Data Feminism investigate hidden infrastructures and power relations. Fairwork, Los Deliveristas Unidos, and city agencies focus on labor conditions, worker rights, and accountability. Meanwhile, delivery platforms design the algorithms, routes, and interfaces that structure the delivery experience. My project sits between these perspectives, combining spatial investigation and interactive visualization to reveal the hidden networks behind an everyday delivery journey.

My position Behind the Route Spatial investigation + interactive visualization

07 · Methods — From research context to a testable case

One specific delivery case becomes a testable spatial experiment.

After defining the research context, I begin with one specific delivery case. I fix one restaurant and one destination near Columbia University. Then I build a street network and generate several possible routes between the same two locations. I compare these routes under different conditions, such as traffic, bicycle infrastructure, weather, waiting time, slope, and access restrictions. I also distinguish between different kinds of evidence: public data, field observation, modeled information, uncertainty, and missing data. This method allows me to move from a general research question to a testable spatial experiment.

Fixed caseOne restaurant → one Columbia-area destination
Experiment protocol Fixed case → street network → route alternatives → conditions → field observation → comparison

08

08 · Computational experiment — The beginning of the simulator

One journey, multiple route logics and hidden infrastructures.

This method becomes a computational experiment called One Journey, Multiple Route Logics. The origin and destination remain the same, but the route changes depending on how the journey is evaluated. One route may be the shortest; another may be faster during traffic; another may use more bicycle lanes; and another may avoid difficult intersections, steep slopes, or restricted entrances. The experiment does not try to identify one universally correct route. Instead, it demonstrates that different priorities and conditions can produce different routes within the same journey. This is the beginning of the simulator.

09 · Visual representation — Layer, compare, and disclose

Visual representation through a situated route map.

To make these differences understandable, the visual strategy follows three principles: layer, compare, and disclose. The routes are placed together so that the viewer can compare their shapes, travel times, and hidden costs. Different visual styles distinguish verified information from modeled information. Solid lines can represent known street data. Dashed lines can represent modeled routes. Transparent areas can show uncertainty. Missing information is not hidden. It is clearly identified. The purpose is not only to show the result, but also to explain how the result was produced.

10 · Rhetorical argument — From certainty to produced conditions

The route is not found.
It is produced.

The platform presents one route and one ETA as simple, predictable, and neutral. The project reveals multiple routes, multiple forms of cost, and incomplete evidence.

Platform presents ONE ROUTE ONE ETA

For the rhetorical argument, the platform presents one route and one ETA. This creates the impression that the delivery journey is simple, predictable, and neutral.

DESIGN
AS ARGUMENT
Project reveals MULTIPLE ROUTES MULTIPLE COSTS

My project presents multiple possible routes, multiple forms of cost, and incomplete evidence. It shows that the final route is shaped by algorithms, workers, streets, buildings, weather, and local restrictions.

Time

Platform ETA often foregrounds moving time while restaurant waiting and campus handoff delay remain less visible.

“Change the definition of cost, and the ‘optimal’ route changes.”
Design position

Route visualization should disclose the assumptions and exclusions behind its calculation instead of presenting one result as inevitable.

11 · Potential capstone — From prototype to critical interface

Two connected parts: a route simulator and a situated route archive.

Provisional direction — not a final solution

The simulator explains how different conditions can produce different routes.
The archive connects those models to real places and lived experiences.
Together, they could help customers, students, designers, researchers, workers, and policymakers better understand the hidden systems behind delivery.
The goal is not to create another delivery platform or a final optimization tool, but to create a critical interface that reveals what existing platforms usually hide.

12

12 · Challenges — What the next stage must resolve

The project still has several challenges.

The first is access to platform and rider data.
The second is validating the modeled routes against real delivery experiences.
The third is involving riders without replacing their knowledge with my own assumptions.
The fourth is keeping the interface clear and understandable.

Challenge 01Data and access
Current gap

Platform dispatch logic, historical rider traces, pricing rules, and performance data are not publicly available.

→
Next step

Maintain a strict evidence protocol, document missing data, and never present authored simulations as platform facts.

Honest position

The project can reconstruct public street conditions, but it cannot yet claim to reproduce real platform decision-making.

NowFunctional route prototypePython · GIS · Mapbox · basic network analysis
Next semesterValidated situated investigationField checks · rider relationships · transparent data practice · visual testing
Next stage

So the next stage is not simply to generate more routes. It is to improve the evidence, test the simulator in a specific location, and connect the computational model more closely to worker experience and field observation.
